generator.params.note: Hand-set from general knowledge of the species: a stemless clump of thick, fleshy, grey-green leaves 30 to 50 cm long (Britton and Millspaugh 1920: 3 dm to 6 dm; a pup's first leaves are far shorter, so the length is not checked over every leaf) and 6 to 7 cm wide at the base, hollowed above and rounded below, with small soft teeth along the margins. Its flowering follows Britton (1918) and Britton and Millspaugh (1920): a stout scape about 0.8 m to 1.2 m high ends in a dense raceme 10 cm to 30 cm long of 40 yellow flowers about 2.5 cm long, drawn as one cluster on the stalk's tip (flowers 1, flower_size 0.22, its look's inflorescence 40 flowers each 0.12 of its length, spread 80, nearly level, on short pedicels 0.03 of its length). Britton (1918) calls the plant stoloniferous, and garden plants crowd with offsets: a crown that flowers may also send out a pup that year, and pups send out up to two of their own (bloom_pup 1, pup_pups 2), so the clump spreads outward. Its stem stays short and hidden: leaves 0.4 mm apart up a stem 1.2 cm thick (internode 0.0004, trunk_radius 0.012), so the 6 leaves a year add under 4 cm in 15 years and the broad leaf bases close over it, where before a 4 cm stem stood bare under each crown as its lower leaves fell. Not fitted to measurements.

allometry.note: Rough heights from general knowledge, with the flowering spike: a quarter metre in its third year, about 0.8 m once it flowers. Wide tolerances.

appearance.note: Colours chosen by eye from photographs, made paler and greyer to match Britton's (1918) 'pale glaucous-green' leaves: grey-green leaves with pale pinkish-white teeth, a grey-green stem and scape, yellow flowers. Its flower laid out whorl by whorl (spec rework P5b): six yellow tepals joined in a tube, six stamens and a superior pistil of three carpels, from the characters of its own and Asphodelaceae's by the rules at the flowering plants. The tepals close into a tube (cup 80, curl 15), the genus's near-cylindric perianth with spreading tips (Britton 1918). Teeth about 1.2 cm apart, within Britton's (1918) 1.3 cm or less, each 3 mm long and turned a little toward the tip. Each leaf is drawn by eye from photographs as thick and fleshy: hollowed along its upper face and rounded below (channelled, 0.55 as thick as wide), widest at its clasping base and keeping its width before it narrows to the tip (taper 0.6), arching out a little (20 degrees) and turning slightly on its length (8 degrees).

traits.note: The Flora of North America's account of the species, as quoted in search results; the page itself was not read: tepals 6, prominently 3-veined, connate basally for half their length; stamens 6, slightly unequal, included to slightly exserted. The Finnish Biodiversity Information Facility calls the perianth tubular, up to 3 cm long (as quoted in search results; the page itself was not read).

traits.height_typical_m.note: Britton and Millspaugh (1920): scape 8 dm to 12 dm high, above a nearly stemless rosette, so a flowering plant stands about that tall.

generator.params.stalk_height.note: Britton (1918), Flora of Bermuda, under Aloe vera: scape stout, 0.6 m to 1.1 m high (2 to 3.5 feet; Britton and Millspaugh 1920 give 8 dm to 12 dm), above a nearly stemless, stoloniferous rosette. Converted from feet; in our own words. The stalk is drawn 0.65 m to the raceme's foot, and the raceme as one cluster above it, so the whole stands about 0.85 m.

generator.params.stalk_head.note: Britton (1918): raceme dense, 10 cm to 30 cm long (4 to 12 inches). The raceme is drawn as one cluster on the stalk's tip (the look's inflorescence), so the stalk's own flowering share is only the node that bears it. The count of 40 flowers is ours, for a dense raceme.

generator.params.flower_angle.note: Britton (1918), for the genus Aloe: flowers nodding in racemes, the perianth near cylindric with its tips somewhat spreading; for Aloe vera, flowers yellow, about 2.5 cm long, on pedicels shorter than their bracts. The raceme stands straight on its stalk (0); within it a flower spreads at 80 degrees, the most a cluster's flower may, so it nearly hangs level.

generator.params.bloom_pup.note: Britton (1918) calls Aloe vera stoloniferous: offsets crowd round the rosette whether or not it flowers, so a flowering crown may also send out a pup (bloom_pup 1), and pups send out up to two of their own (pup_pups 2, ours), so the clump spreads outward.
